Almost. Lower temperature sharpens the output distribution, so the model picks the most likely token instead of sampling far down the list. For factual answers grounded in retrieved chunks, that means fewer fluent but invented details. Your one sentence: lower temperature favors the likeliest token, which keeps grounded answers faithful. Voted Big-O. I can trace recursion but I cannot tell O(n log n) from O(n^2) to save my life.
Voted sorting. Why does quicksort usually win if worst case is O(n^2)?

It works until it doesn't. Without a base case the calls never stop, and Python ends that with RecursionError around call 1000. Your tests were just small enough to survive. Add the base case, then try sum of 2000 and watch what happens.
Did exactly this on HW3. Worked on 10 items, died on 500. The error message is how I learned what a stack is.

Both answers at once: closed book, pen only. Scope is tracing plus Big-O through Chapter 5. Sorting is midterm-only.
Number two was mine. Walked to the target instead of before it, every delete off by one.
Empty-list case got me too. Null check first, always.

Because worst case needs a villain: already-sorted input plus a naive first-element pivot. Random or median-of-three pivots make that vanishingly rare, and then quicksort wins on constants: it sorts in place with great cache behavior while mergesort allocates and copies. O(n log n) average with small constants beats O(n log n) with big ones. Review session will trace one partition live.
The constants part is what I was missing. See you Friday.

Ask what the loops do. Nested loops over all n each: n times n, O(n^2). One loop that halves the problem each pass, like binary search: about log n passes. n work per level times log n levels: O(n log n), which is mergesort and the good quicksort. Count the levels, multiply by the work per level. Try it on the HW4 reverse first: single pass, O(n).
Levels times work per level. Writing that on my cheat sheet verbatim.
